sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a common complication following major surgery, occurring in 15%–72% of patients. PSD poses a significant threat to both postoperative recovery and long-term outcome, leading to elevated risks of cognitive decline, pain sensitivity and cardiovascular events in patients. The current pharmacological treatments for PSD are typically reactive, administered only after symptoms have manifested, highlighting a critical unmet need for effective prophylactic strategies during the perioperative period. Recently, an increasing number of studies have demonstrated the effect of esketamine on preventing PSD, but their findings are inconsistent. This protocol outlines a systematic review and meta-analysis to examine the effect of perioperative esketamine on the prevention of PSD.

sec.title: Methods and analysis
sec.p: A comprehensive search will be conducted in MEDLINE (via Ovid), EMBASE (via Ovid), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (via Ovid), PubMed and Web of Science by two authors independently. The search terms will comprise indexed and free-text terms to encompass the concepts of esketamine and PSD. The primary outcome is the incidence of PSD at postoperative days 1, 3 and 7. Two authors will independently conduct study screening, data extraction and risk of bias assessment with the Cochrane Collaboration’s tool. RevMan V.5.4.1 and Stata V.17.0 software will be used to conduct the statistical analysis. Subgroup analysis, sensitivity analysis and assessment of publication bias will be performed to verify the strength of our conclusions. Finally, the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach will be used to recommend evidence quality.

sec.title: Ethics and dissemination
sec.p: Ethical approval is not required for this study. The findings will be presented at national or international conferences and submitted to a peer-reviewed journal.

caption.title: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY

list-item.p: This study is guided by Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols statement.
Comprehensive outcomes will be collected and evaluated to determine the efficacy and safety of perioperative esketamine administration.
Subgroup and sensitivity analyses will be used to assess the robustness of the pooled results.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Sleep disorders affect over 20% of the global population, with the prevalence exceeding 50% among the elderly.1 2 Postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD) is a frequent complication of surgery, with its incidence and severity often correlating with the severity of surgical trauma.3 Although the disruption of sleep architecture—specifically the suppression of rapid eye movement and slow-wave sleep—is more profound in major surgery than in minor procedures, PSD remains a significant concern across the surgical spectrum.4 5 Affected patients commonly experience diminished sleep quality and duration, early awakening, frequent nightmares, sleep terrors and sleep-related breathing disorders.3 6 Occurring in 15%–72% of patients after surgery, PSD is closely associated with impaired postoperative recovery, which includes poorer cognitive function, increased pain sensitivity and a heightened risk of cardiovascular events.7,10 Recent studies highlight the importance of a multimodal approach to PSD treatment and the ongoing pursuit of effective therapies. The multiple approaches include non-pharmacological interventions, such as minimising surgical trauma by choosing laparoscopic over open-abdominal surgery, and eliminating ambient stressors at night;11 12 and pharmacological strategies, such as reducing opioid consumption or administering agents like zolpidem, melatonin and dexmedetomidine when necessary.1113,15 However, a recent meta-analysis indicated that the evidence regarding the efficacy of these strategies for sleep quality enhancement is inadequate.16

Esketamine is the S-enantiomer of racemic ketamine and a novel N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist, which demonstrates a greater receptor affinity than ketamine, resulting in stronger anaesthetic and analgesic properties as well as a reduced side-effect burden.17 18 Esketamine, administered intravenously at subanaesthetic doses, is reported to exhibit rapid and robust antidepressant effects in patients with postpartum depression, bipolar depression or treatment-resistant depression.19 20 PSD frequently co-occurs with depression in surgical patients. Accumulating research underscores the therapeutic benefit of esketamine for sleep quality improvement in patients suffering from both depression and sleep disturbances.21 22 Recent years have seen a steady stream of studies investigating the effect of esketamine on PSD following general anaesthesia. The results, however, have been inconsistent.723,26 Therefore, to address these conflicting findings, a systematic review and meta-analysis is warranted to consolidate existing research and provide conclusive evidence on the impact of esketamine on PSD.

sec.title: Study registration
sec.p: This protocol was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) statement,27 28 which is provided as an online supplementary PRISMA-P-checklist (online supplemental file 1) and was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) database (CRD420251232636). The systematic review will be conducted following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and reported in accordance with the PRISMA statement.29 The systematic review is planned to commence on 1 March 2026 and is expected to be completed by 1 September 2026.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: Two authors (HY and SW) will independently search the electronic databases including PubMed, MEDLINE (via Ovid), EMBASE (via Ovid) and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (via Ovid) from inception to 1 March 2026 to identify eligible studies. Additionally, the Web of Science and the US clinical trials registry (https://clinicaltrials.gov/) will also be searched for in-progress or completed clinical trials. The search terms will comprise both Medical Subject Headings and free-text terms, including esketamine, L-Ketamine, S-Ketamine, (-)-Ketamine, sleep, sleep disorder, sleep disturbance, sleep quality, postoperative sleep disorder, postoperative sleep disturbance, sleep initiation and maintenance disorders and randomized controlled trial. Furthermore, the references cited in all eligible studies will be scrutinised to identify additional potentially relevant studies. Any discrepancies between the two authors will be resolved with the assistance of the senior researcher (HH). The detailed search strategy for all databases is available online (online supplemental file 2). Throughout the entire process of conducting this meta-analysis, we will conduct periodic searches of the databases to identify any newly published eligible studies.

sec.title: Inclusion and exclusion criteria of studies
sec.p: The inclusion criteria were established based on the PICOS framework.30 Studies will be included when meeting the following criteria:

list-item.p: Participants: Adult patients receiving any kinds of surgeries under general anaesthesia.
Interventions: Perioperative esketamine administration through single intravenous injection or continuous intravenous infusion.
Comparison: Patients in the control group received the same volume of normal saline or other drugs.

Outcome measures: The primary outcome will be the incidence of PSD at postoperative days 1, 3 and 7. PSD is defined as Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) score of 6 or higher or Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS) score of 6 or higher. The NRS scores, AIS scores, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores and Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire scores within the first 3 postoperative days will be categorised as secondary outcomes. Other secondary outcomes include anxiety and depression scores on postoperative days 1 and 3 evaluated by Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale; the Visual Analogue Scale or NRS pain score at rest and movement at 1 hour, 2 hours, 6 hours, 12 hours, 24 hours, 48 hours and 72 hours after surgery; postoperative opioid consumption calculated as morphine equivalent, the incidence of postoperative rescue analgesia; Quality of Recovery-15 score measured at postoperative days 1, 2, 3 and 7; the incidence of postoperative delirium within the first 3 postoperative days; the serum levels of interleukin-6 at 24 hours postoperatively, and anaesthesia or surgery related outcome: intraoperative opioid consumption calculated as morphine equivalent, surgery or anaesthesia duration, extubation time, length of stay in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU). Adverse events primarily encompass anaesthesia-related complications, spanning both the intraoperative and postoperative periods. The intraoperative complications are mainly haemodynamic parameters, such as hypotension, hypertension, tachycardia and bradycardia. Postoperative complications primarily encompass drug-specific adverse reactions, categorised into psychiatric manifestations (hallucination, nightmare, agitation), neurological symptoms (dizziness, diplopia, somnolence) and other general adverse events (post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV), hypoxaemia, itching).

sec.p: Studies not meeting the above-mentioned criteria, or studies with paediatric populations or combined drugs such as dexmedetomidine, will be excluded.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: Two authors (HY and SW) will review all titles and abstracts of all the retrieved literature to eliminate irrelevant and duplicate studies independently. Following this initial screening, the same authors will evaluate the full texts of all candidate studies using predefined eligibility criteria. Any discrepancies between the two authors will be resolved with the assistance of the senior researcher (HH). The flow diagram detailing the study selection process is presented in figure 1.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: Using a predesigned datasheet, two independent reviewers (HY and SW) will systematically extract data encompassing the following variables: (1) study characteristics, including trial title, journal name, first author, year of publication, sample size, country of study, type of surgery; (2) demographic data, such as sex and age of participants; (3) intervention details, such as dosage, administration routes and patient groups; (4) primary outcomes, secondary outcomes and adverse events. Disagreements will be resolved by discussion with the senior researcher (HH).

sec.title: Risk of bias assessment
sec.p: Two authors (HY and SW) independently will evaluate the risk of bias (RoB) in RCTs via the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool (Cochrane Collaboration, UK).31 This tool consists of the following six domains: (1) bias arising from the random sequence generation (selection bias), (2) bias due to allocation concealment (selection bias), (3) bias due to blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias), (4) bias due to incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), (5) bias due to selective outcome reporting (reporting bias) and (6) any other potential sources of bias.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses for this meta-analysis will be performed using RevMan (V.5.4.1, the Cochrane Collaboration) and Stata (V.17.0, StataCorp). Continuous outcomes will be presented as mean differences with 95% CIs and binary outcomes as ORs with 95% CIs. Statistical heterogeneity will be assessed using the χ² test (with a significance threshold of p<0.10) and the I² statistic. An I² value ≥50% or a significant χ² test indicates substantial heterogeneity, in which case a random-effects model will be applied; otherwise, a fixed-effects model will be used to generate the forest plots.32 Beyond statistical considerations, we recognise that numerous patient-related, anaesthesia-related and surgery-related factors (eg, age of patients, anaesthesia management, surgery type) significantly modulate postoperative sleep quality. Therefore, even if the I2 is less than 50%, subgroup analyses for these key clinical variables will still be conducted. This approach allows us to evaluate the impact of different clinical settings on the efficacy of esketamine and to ensure the stability and generalisability of the findings. If clinical, methodological or statistical heterogeneity is too high to allow for a meaningful meta-analysis, a narrative synthesis following the SWiM (Synthesis Without Meta-analysis) reporting guidelines33 will be performed.

sec.title: Missing data
sec.p: When literature data is missing, we will reach out to the corresponding authors via telephone, email or other means to obtain the missing information. Before receiving accurate responses, we will not use any statistical method to analyse the data. If no response was received, outcome data will be extracted from graphs using Plot Digitizer (http://plotdigitizer.sourceforge.net/).34

sec.title: Publication bias assessment
sec.p: The assessment for publication bias will be based on outcomes that included a minimum of 10 studies. Following Cochrane guidelines, we will perform a visual inspection of funnel plots and use Egger’s test for statistical analysis, where a p value <0.05 suggested potential bias.30 35

sec.title: Assessment and management of heterogeneity
sec.p: To address potential heterogeneity arising from diverse patient-related, surgery-related and anaesthesia-related factors, a multifaceted strategy will be employed. We will primarily conduct prespecified subgroup analyses to explore the impact of key determinants on the efficacy of esketamine in improving postoperative sleep quality, including patient demographics (elderly vs non-elderly), surgical characteristics (cardiac vs non-cardiac; major vs minor surgery, where major surgery is defined as a surgical duration exceeding 2 hours36) and anaesthetic management (propofol vs volatile maintenance; opioid-free vs opioid-inclusive anaesthesia; general anaesthesia alone vs general anaesthesia combined with regional anaesthesia). Furthermore, intervention-related variables such as the timepoint of esketamine administration (pre-induction use, intraoperative use or postoperative use), dosage (low-dose vs sub-anaesthetic dose) and mode of esketamine administration (single injection vs continuous infusion) will be scrutinised. Should a sufficient number of studies (n>10) be available, meta-regression will be performed to statistically evaluate the influence of continuous variables on the primary outcome. Finally, the robustness of the pooled results and the sources of heterogeneity will be assessed through leave-one-out sensitivity analyses using Stata V.17.0.

sec.title: Grading the quality of evidence
sec.p: The quality of evidence will be evaluated using the GRADE guidelines, which refer to the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation, and is categorised as high, moderate, low or very low. This categorisation is based on an assessment of five domains: RoB, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias.37 38

sec.title: Patient and public involvement
sec.p: Patients or the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination plans of our research.

sec.title: Ethics and dissemination
sec.p: Ethical approval is not required for this study. The findings will be presented at national or international conferences and submitted to a peer-reviewed journal. For inquiries regarding research integrity, please contact HH, Deputy Head of the Department of Anesthesiology, West China Second University Hospital, Sichuan University, at han.huang@scu.edu.cn.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This protocol delineates a systematic review and meta-analysis that seeks to evaluate the efficacy of esketamine in mitigating PSD. This study will address a critical evidence gap in the current literature. Despite a growing interest in the potential of esketamine for managing PSD, the existing body of evidence remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis will therefore aim to provide the consolidated, high-level evidence regarding the impact of esketamine on PSD.

PSD is a multifactorial challenge that undermines postoperative recovery and may adversely affect long-term outcomes. Current multimodal management strategies often lack robust pharmacological options with a favourable safety profile. If the efficacy of esketamine for PSD is confirmed, it could become a valuable component of enhanced recovery protocol, which will provide clinicians with a novel and evidence-backed option to improve patient comfort and in-hospital recovery trajectories. Furthermore, by improving early postoperative recovery, esketamine may have the potential to positively influence long-term patient outcomes. PSD has been associated with an increased risk of persistent pain, cognitive decline and even cardiovascular morbidity. Therefore, an effective intervention for PSD in the immediate postoperative period may not only enhance short-term convalescence but also act as a protective factor against these deleterious sequelae, ultimately promoting a higher quality of life and functional status long after discharge.

However, we recognise that PSD is a complex phenomenon influenced by multiple factors, such as anaesthesia management, severity of surgical trauma, age of patients and postoperative analgesia. Such clinical heterogeneity across studies may impact the generalisability of our findings. Therefore, rather than providing a single pooled estimate, our study will focus on exploring these potential sources of variation through predefined subgroup analyses and meta-regression. This approach aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of esketamine’s efficacy across different clinical contexts and offer a more reliable reference for perioperative sleep management.

In summary, PSD is an urgent clinical issue that demands attention. This meta-analysis will help determine whether esketamine has any potential benefits, thereby providing robust evidence to guide clinical practice and inform the design of future trials.
